newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Protestors block soya shipment to Antwerp port.
newsitem.headline: Protestors block soya shipment to Antwerp port.

text.p: Greenpeace environmentalists stepped up their protest against genetically altered soybeans on Thursday by stopping a Polish bulk carrier it believed had the beans on board from docking at the Belgian port of Antwerp.
Inflatable dinghies blocked the ship in a lock on the approach to the port, and four activists chained themselves to a drawbridge at the port entrance to prevent it opening.
Protesters had hung a banner reading "genetic experiment - don't buy it," though the atmosphere at the scene remained calm.

In a statement Greenpeace said the Polish-registerd Ziemia Zamojska was carrying a U.S. grain shipment which left Cleveland, Ohio on October 8, and that Greenpeace had stopped it from unloading in Antwerp at the wharf of U.S. grain multinational Cargill.
It said the ship was believed to be carrying the new type of bean which has been developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto to be resistant to its own new "super weedkiller" Roundup.
Environmental groups describe the Roundup technology as a risky experiment with nature.
But the new Monsanto strain has been given a clean bill of health by the authorities in the United States and European Union, who say it poses no danger to the human food chain.

Greenpeace said it had received a letter from Cargill in which the company said there were soybeans on board the Ziemia Zamojska but could not "confirm or deny the presence of Roundup Ready soybeans because these beans are not separated from traditional soybeans at harvest."
"Greenpeace is calling on Cargill to demand the segregation of the soya and to reject further shipments of the genetically engineered beans," the environmentalist's statement said.

Amsterdam-based Greenpeace International has vowed to keep up a campaign of direct action against the imports after blocking what it believed was the first shipment in a freighter, the Ideal Progress, in Hamburg on Tuesday.
Police later intervened and the ship and its cargo of 44,600 tonnes of U.S. soybeans docked successfully.
Several more vessels are expected to arrive in the ports of Ghent and Rotterdam over the coming weeks.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety even though they consider it safe.
